extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in research integrity, scholarly publishing professionals, journal editors, sleuths and academic researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A monthly news roundup about retractions, publishing fraud, and research-integrity issues across disciplines, summarizing cases and lessons for publishers, editors, and researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation accuracy and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Made-up citations can indicate the use of generative AI; the paper contained irrelevant, and in some cases nonexistent, references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check references for existence and relevance; watch for fabricated citations as a red flag for AI-generated or sloppy manuscripts. Example: a study of the Brazilian coastline with no citations of work conducted in Brazil or by researchers who had previously worked in the region was suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and affiliation plausibility/transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: All listed authors on a Brazil-focused study had affiliations in India, an odd detail that raised suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that author affiliations are consistent with the study context and investigate unexpected patterns (e.g., all authors affiliated with locations unrelated to the study region). Contact editors or corresponding authors when affiliations seem implausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image integrity (no duplication or inappropriate reuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles were retracted because images and figures appeared similar or identical to others in the same paper or published elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen figures for duplication within a paper and against published literature; use image-forensics and reverse-image-search tools. Identical or highly similar images across different publications are grounds for concern and possible retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability of analyses and correctness of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper was retracted 'because the authors’ analyses could not be replicated and multiple errors were identified.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure methods and data are reported with sufficient detail for replication; require access to data/code where appropriate. Lack of replicability and multiple analytical errors justify correction or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and authenticity of images (avoidance of plagiarized or joke sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: An altered image originally posted as an April Fool’s joke was used as a figure in a published paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the provenance of images and figures (reverse-image search, check original sources). Do not use images from joke, fictional, or uncredited sources; using such images is misconduct and may lead to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer/identity verification beyond institutional email
rubrics_metrics.description: University email addresses are no longer an effective bulwark against fake peer review; bad actors used round-trip-verified institutional-domain emails to impersonate reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on institutional email addresses to authenticate reviewers or authors. Implement stronger identity-verification procedures (e.g., ORCID checks, institutional confirmations, multi-factor verification) to prevent fake-peer-review schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and mitigation of metrics gaming and other fraudulent publishing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraudulent publishing in math (and other fields) includes metrics gaming; working groups produced lists of recommendations to detect and deal with that problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor suspicious publication patterns (e.g., large numbers of minimally substantive papers, unusual citation patterns), adopt community recommendations to detect gaming, and develop processes to investigate and sanction fraudulent behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based public allegations and cautious use of insinuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Taylor & Francis threatened legal action against an anonymous group whose allegations were based largely on vague insinuations rather than evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public accusations about researchers, publishers, or integrity failures should be supported by clear evidence. Anonymous groups and investigators should avoid publishing vague insinuations to reduce legal exposure and maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and transparency of retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors objected to a retraction and pointed to flaws in the published notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices should be clear, accurate, and transparent about reasons for retraction. Publishers should ensure notices are defensible and provide sufficient detail to explain the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutiny of high-impact papers and public-health-relevant findings
rubrics_metrics.description: A widely viewed and highly cited paper (e.g., vitamin D and COVID-19) that influenced the public was later retracted after critics flagged data concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers with large public reach or policy/clinical implications merit extra scrutiny (robust peer review, data checks). Rapid dissemination increases the harm of flawed results, so mechanisms for post-publication review and swift correction are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of curated tools/databases to screen journals and track retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Resources such as the Retraction Watch Database and the Retraction Watch Hijacked Journal Checker help identify problematic journals and track retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers, editors, and authors should consult established databases and screening tools to flag hijacked or questionable journals and to research an author’s or journal’s retraction history during editorial checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern analysis of author behaviour and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors with many papers and multiple retractions (example: two researchers with eight retractions across decades) raise concerns about patterns of problematic conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate patterns across an author's corpus (frequency of retractions, similarity of problems) as part of integrity assessments; persistent patterns may indicate systemic misconduct and warrant institutional investigation.
